Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Sofia Reyes, twenty-seven, American of Latin American descent, returned from her detention with a quiet but permanent recalibration of her surroundings. The event itself was defined by a single, relentless presence: a woman who controlled every aspect of the room with minimal words and maximal authority. There were no windows, no loose floorboards, and no moment when the heavy steel door clicked open without the woman's deliberate signal. When Sofia was secured to a metal chair with wide canvas straps, she learned the exact geometry of having no options. Her wrists bore raw, red abrasions for days afterward, and she remembers now how the sight of fresh injuries on her own skin mirrored the cold certainty that she would remain exactly where she was placed until someone else decided otherwise. The female interrogator's steady posture and unbroken gaze left an imprint that still shapes how Sofia navigates her present. In the months that followed, her daily life became a series of carefully measured thresholds. She found herself lingering at her apartment door long after the latch engaged, turning the deadbolt twice, listening to the dead silence of the hallway before repeating the motion to be certain. Sleep offered no predictable refuge; she would wake in the dark with her breath shallow, certain that the stillness meant she was no longer safe. She would sit upright, pressing her palms to her knees, waiting for the familiar jolt of surprise to settle each time a pipe groaned or a car passed outside. When the recall came, it arrived as a sudden, heavy pressure behind her eyes. She would feel so overwhelmed by the flood of it that she had to set down her phone, step away from her desk, and walk to the kitchen sink. The shame that accompanied the memory was not a fleeting thought but a persistent weight. She noticed how the recollection felt entirely separate from her, as if the woman who lived through it belonged to a stranger. Alongside these internal experiences, she had come to believe that harm could arrive from anyone, without warning or pattern. She could no longer trust that she would make the right call if faced with a sudden choice. The conviction that she had permanently changed for the worse settled quietly in her routine. She found herself hesitant when clients asked for her assessment or when supervisors handed her a new work order. Her occupation as an HVAC technician required constant negotiation with these thresholds. During a midsummer service call, she entered a cramped residential utility closet to diagnose a tripped compressor. The door clicked shut behind her, leaving her alone with a female homeowner in a space too narrow to step backward. The client's sleeve had ridden up, exposing a raised, pink scar across her forearm, and Sofia felt her breathing tighten as she knelt beside the mechanical panel. She completed the electrical continuity test with steady hands, but her attention remained anchored to the confined dimensions of the doorway and the woman's unbroken stance beside her. She had learned to recognize the familiar pressure of having no options, even when the situation was entirely different. That moment crystallized a shift in her work pattern: she now requests a co-technician for residential calls, trading solo routes for paired assignments to ensure she is never positioned in a narrow space with a single woman. The cumulative weight of checking her locks, waking in the dark, and bracing for sudden confrontations finally prompted her to schedule an intake. She did not know if sessions could soften the edges of what she carried, but she hoped to stop waiting for the door to open.
